name: Gluconolactone

lead: Gluconolactone (glucono-delta-lactone) is a glucose derivative also used as a food additive (E575). In skincare it is sold as a polyhydroxy acid and pitched at sensitive skin as a gentler alternative to glycolic acid, loosening dead cells for a smoother, more even surface.

Published skin studies are few. Small comparisons report effects broadly similar to alpha hydroxy acids with less stinging in some, and in-vitro data show reduced UV-induced elastin damage. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review concluded in 2022 that it is safe at reported use concentrations.

paras: It is used in toners, serums and mild peels on a regular routine. In water it partly converts to gluconic acid, so acidity develops gradually, and it is also described as a humectant and chelating agent.
Described as well tolerated at cosmetic-use levels. Large oral doses act as a laxative. As with other exfoliating acids, sun protection is generally advised.

label.generic: CITRIC ACID, GLUCONOLACTONE AND MAGNESIUM CARBONATE

chain: Dead cells loosen with low irritation
angle.text: Gluconolactone is a polyhydroxy acid used for gentle exfoliation, especially by people whose skin reacts to glycolic acid. It loosens dead cells with low irritation for a smoother, more even surface; small trials compare it with glycolic acid and report less irritation.

lead: Gluconolactone, also called glucono-delta-lactone (GDL), is the cyclic ester of D-gluconic acid, made from glucose oxidation.[1] It is approved as a food additive (E575) used as an acidifier, sequestrant and leavening or curing agent.[1][2]

In cosmetics it is classed as a polyhydroxy acid (PHA) and used as a skin-conditioning and chelating ingredient, marketed for exfoliation with a lower reported irritation than alpha hydroxy acids.[2] The small clinical literature includes comparisons with glycolic acid and benzoyl peroxide.[2]
infobox: Polyhydroxy acid; lactone of gluconic acid

paras: GDL is a white, nearly odourless crystalline powder, typically produced by glucose oxidase action or fermentation of glucose.[1][2] In water it hydrolyses gradually toward gluconic acid until an equilibrium is reached, so a fresh solution grows more acidic over about two hours; heat and high pH accelerate the process.[1][2]

Brands market it for gentle exfoliation, hydration and use on sensitive or acne-prone skin.[2] Grokipedia states that older trials classed it as an alpha hydroxy acid and a 2004 review grouped it with lactobionic acid as a PHA with humectant and antioxidant properties.[2]

As E575 it is used in tofu coagulation, dairy, cured meats and baking.[2] A combination of citric acid, gluconolactone and magnesium carbonate (Renacidin) is a US-labelled irrigation solution for dissolving certain bladder stones and preventing catheter encrustation.[3]

A small number of skin studies are described secondhand. According to Grokipedia, an 8% gluconolactone regimen performed similarly to glycolic, lactic and tartaric acids on barrier measures, and caused less irritation after a detergent challenge than some comparators; a 12-week photoaging comparison with glycolic acid found both improved features, with glycolic acid ahead on some measures and causing more stinging; and a 150-patient double-blind acne trial compared 14% gluconolactone with 5% benzoyl peroxide, with both reducing lesions and fewer side effects reported for gluconolactone.[2] These descriptions come from an AI-generated summary and the underlying trials were not independently reviewed here. A registered trial of topical antioxidant agents in photodamaged skin also exists but is not specific to gluconolactone.[4]

Grokipedia reports that the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded in 2022 that gluconolactone is safe at the concentrations in use, including up to 15% in leave-on products, and that patch tests found no irritation or sensitisation.[2] Single oral doses above about 20 g have caused laxative effects in humans.[2] The Renacidin label lists bladder irritation and chemical cystitis in about 3% of patients, a distinct irrigation use.[3] For AHAs generally, regulators have noted possible increased sun sensitivity.[5]
